'''''Cerastium glomeratum''''' is a species of flowering plant in the family [[Caryophyllaceae]] known by the common names '''sticky mouse-ear chickweed''' and '''clammy chickweed'''. It is native to Europe, Macaronesia to Assam but is known on most continents as an [[introduced species]].<ref name=powo>{{cite web |work=Plants of the World Online |title=''Cerastium glomeratum'' Thuill. |publisher=Royal Botanic Garden, Kew |url=https://powo.science.kew.org/taxon/urn:lsid:ipni.org:names:152274-1 |access-date=16 April 2023 }}</ref> It grows in many types of habitat. The blooming period is February, March, April, and May.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.calflora.org/cgi-bin/species_query.cgi?where-calrecnum=1873|title=Calflora: Cerastium glomeratum|website=www.calflora.org|language=en|access-date=2017-05-10}}</ref>

==Description==
[[File:CerastiumG3.jpg|thumb|The upper stem and flowers are covered in glandular hairs.]]
This is an annual herb growing from a slender [[taproot]]. It produces a branched stem up to {{Convert|45|cm|sp=us}} tall, with abundant glandular and non-glandular hairs. The leaves are opposite, hairy, up to 2 cm long, and the basal ones typically die back before flowering. The bracts are green, hairy and generally similar to the leaves.

The [[inflorescence]] bears as few as 3 or as many as 50 small, dioecious flowers arranged in a cyme and borne on very short pedicels. Each flower has 5 hairy green [[sepals]] which are occasionally red-tipped, and 5 white bifid petals which are a few millimeters long and generally about the same length as the sepals. The fruit is a capsule less than a centimeter long which is tipped with ten tiny teeth.<ref name="Stace" /><ref name="Parnell">Parnell, J. and Curtis, T. 2012 ''Webb's An Irish Flora.'' Cork University Press. {{ISBN|978-185918-4783}}</ref>

==Identification==
[[File:Cerastium glomeratum inflorescence.jpg|thumb|The flowers of sticky mouse-ear are often bunched together, on short stalks.]]
This plant usually has abundant glandular hairs towards the top of the stem and on the sepals. Because it is an annual, plants are easily uprooted and every stem develops flowers. The flowers are also borne on very short pedicels (stalks), so they tend to occur in tight clusters.<ref name=Stace>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=New Flora of the British Isles |date=2019 |location=Suffolk |isbn=978-1-5272-2630-2}}</ref>

==Taxonomy==
It was named by Jean Louis Thuillier in his "Flore des Environs de Paris" (1800). Many synonyms have been coined over the years, which are listed in the [https://www.gbif.org/dataset/be1f0e7a-0ee0-45a8-847c-9d12e3997425 Synonymic Checklists of the Vascular plants of the World]. Many forms, varieties and subspecies have also been named, but none is now widely accepted. It is not known to hybridise with any other species.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Stace |first1=C.A. |title=Hybridization and the Flora of the British Isles |date=1975 |publisher=Academic Press |location=London |isbn=0-12-661650-7}}</ref>

Its chromosome number is 2n=72.<ref name="Stace" />

==Habitat==
Frequent in waste places,<ref name="Parnell"/> walls, banks and arable land.<ref>Hackney, P. (editor) 1992. ''Stewart & Corry's Flora of the North-east of Ireland''. Institute of Irish Studies, The Queen's University of Belfast. {{ISBN|0-85389-446-9}}</ref><ref>Clapham, A.R., Tutin, T.G. and Warburg, E.F. 1968. ''Excursion Flora of the British Isles''. Second edition. Cambridge University Press.</ref>

==Uses==
The leaves and shoots were used as a wild food in ancient China.<ref>Read. B.E. (1977) ''Famine Foods of the [[Jiuhuang Bencao|Chiu-Huang Pen-ts'ao]]''. Southern Materials Centre, Taipei.</ref> In Nepal, the juice of this plant was applied to the forehead to relieve headaches. The juice could also be dropped into the nostrils to treat nosebleeds.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.pfaf.org/user/Plant.aspx?LatinName=Cerastium+glomeratum|title=Cerastium glomeratum sticky chickweed PFAF Plant Database|website=www.pfaf.org|access-date=2017-05-10}}</ref>

The leaves can also be boiled and eaten.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Niering |first1=William A. |authorlink1=William Niering| last2=Olmstead |first2=Nancy C. |title=The Audubon Society Field Guide to North American Wildflowers, Eastern Region |year=1985 |orig-date=1979|publisher=Knopf |isbn=0-394-50432-1 |page=455}}</ref>
